quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: in the second quarter IBM delivered 1% revenue growth (constant currency), 30 basis points of operating pre-tax margin expansion and 5% diluted operating earnings per share growth; operating gross profit margins were down 70 basis points on the revenue shortfall and mix, while adjusted EBITDA and operating pre-tax margins expanded 20 and 30 basis points. Segment profit margin expanded 160 basis points in IBM Consulting and 110 basis points in IBM Software and declined 150 basis points in Infrastructure (IBM Z mix headwind). Through the first half IBM generated $4.8 billion of free cash flow, flat year over year (about $700 million increase in adjusted EBITDA, offset by inventory, higher cash taxes and net interest expense). CEO Arvind Krishna: the second quarter 'fell short of expectations'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue +1%; operating pre-tax margin +30 basis points; operating EPS +5%; 1H free cash flow $4.8 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: in the final weeks of June many clients redirected spending towards servers, storage and memory purchases to secure supply-constrained infrastructure ahead of expected price increases, so tens of large deals failed to close on the expected timelines, accounting for the majority of the shortfall. CEO Arvind Krishna: clients' alternate purchases were 'increasing 30% in dollar value quarter-to-quarter'; about 400 to 500 of the miss was in software; about a third of the slipped large CapEx deals (in the low tens) already closed in the first three weeks of the third quarter, 'a indication, not yet full evidence' that the demand was deferred, not destroyed (normally IBM would expect two-thirds to three-fourths of them to close over the next six months). CFO: 'We haven't really lost maybe one of the deals, maybe two.'
quarterly_data.figure: clients' alternate purchases +30% in dollar value quarter-to-quarter; about a third of slipped deals closed in three weeks

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: Software revenue grew 5% with flat organic growth; transaction processing declined 9% (enterprise license agreement timing), data grew 18% and automation 3%. About 80% of annual software revenue is recurring and ARR was $24.6 billion, up 8%; transactional revenue (the other 20%) was down high single digits. Red Hat growth accelerated one point sequentially to 11%; OpenShift ARR is $2.2 billion, with about $680 million of containerization and virtualization contracts signed since early 2024; HashiCorp had another record bookings quarter; Confluent is on track after its first full quarter post-close; RHEL performance continued to be impacted by constrained hardware availability. CEO Arvind Krishna: software is nearly 45% of total revenue and the shortfall was limited to a CapEx-sensitive area of the portfolio.
quarterly_data.figure: Software +5% (TP -9%, data +18%, automation +3%); ARR $24.6 billion (+8%); Red Hat +11%; OpenShift ARR $2.2 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: Infrastructure revenue declined 7%; mainframe was down 42%, off 70% growth in last year's launch quarter (mainframe is always down in the fifth quarter of a cycle) and below IBM's expectations, yet z17 is at nearly 130% program to program, about $1 billion more mainframe revenue and $3+ billion more software stack than at the same point of the z16 cycle; nearly 50% of z17 customers are investing in AI capabilities with the Spyre Accelerator. CEO Arvind Krishna: Distributed Infrastructure delivered its best quarter of revenue growth on record, growing 37%; Power11 is gaining momentum and IBM is gaining share in Storage; earlier this month IBM introduced a smaller LinuxONE system; 'we see no evidence of clients moving off the mainframe'.
quarterly_data.figure: Infrastructure -7%; mainframe -42%; z17 nearly 130% program to program; Distributed Infrastructure +37%

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: IBM exited the quarter with approximately $500 million of Distributed Infrastructure (Power and Storage) backlog, its highest on record. In Consulting, signings grew 6% (second consecutive quarter of growth) and revenue grew 1%; generative AI represented about 50% of signings in the quarter and now makes up over 30% of the consulting backlog.
quarterly_data.figure: Distributed Infrastructure backlog approximately $500 million (record); Consulting signings +6%; GenAI about 50% of signings, over 30% of backlog

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Jim Kavanaugh: given the constrained infrastructure supply environment, IBM proactively strengthened its supply chain through the first half with buy-aheads 'at economically prudent prices' to address the demand it sees in Distributed Infrastructure, Power and Storage; inventory exiting the first half was up $600 million year to year and is expected to flush through as a second-half tailwind; IBM continues to secure inventory and accelerate its supply chain. CEO Arvind Krishna: IBM has held its price so far in July and has not taken increases, 'nowhere near as aggressive as some of the alternate infrastructure providers'.
quarterly_data.figure: inventory up $600 million year to year at end of 1H

quarterly_data.signal: IBM now expects 2026 revenue growth in a range of 4%-5% at constant currency (CFO: the low end is 'our base case', about a 1 point plus takedown); software growth revised to 6%-8%; infrastructure now expected to grow low single digits (CFO: up about 2 points guide to guide); consulting low to mid-single-digit growth; free cash flow growth of about $1 billion maintained; 100 basis points of operating pre-tax margin expansion; operating tax rate in the mid-teens. Third quarter: constant-currency revenue growth consistent with the full year, currency a 1.5 point headwind, operating pre-tax margin similar to the second quarter. CFO: recurring software revenue growth went from 7% in the first quarter to 8% in the second and is expected to reach about 10% in the second half; transaction processing assumed down low to mid-single digits in the second half.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 revenue growth 4%-5%; software 6%-8%; free cash flow +about $1 billion; operating pre-tax margin +100 basis points; Q3 currency headwind 1.5 points

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Arvind Krishna: 'complete conviction in the double-digit long-term software growth'; the recurring/transactional software mix of 80/20 'used to be 60/40', and IBM is investing in capabilities that grow at 15%-20% (HashiCorp and Confluent accelerated after acquisition, watsonx growing faster than the aggregate). CFO Jim Kavanaugh: every dollar of mainframe hardware lands $3+ of software; IBM Z handles 450 billion inferences per day at 1 ms, installed MIPS are growing 15%-20% program to date, clients deploying watsonx Code Assistant for Z grow MIPS capacity three times faster, and clients see a 2 to 15x total cost of ownership advantage on the mainframe. CEO: IBM Z runs over 70% of the world's transaction volume by value across over 140 million installed MIPS, with clients representing 85% of installed MIPS maintaining or growing capacity.
quarterly_data.figure: long-term software growth double-digit target; $3+ software per mainframe hardware dollar; 450 billion inferences per day; 140 million installed MIPS

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Arvind Krishna: IBM launched Lightwell, through which clients subscribe for $1 million per year to access open-source packages that have been remediated or validated, a TAM for IBM and Red Hat (the Mythos release in early April accelerated the discovery of security vulnerabilities); more than 7,500 package versions were made available in the first two weeks, on top of the 30,000 packages IBM already handles with Linux, HashiCorp, Confluent, Kubernetes and OpenShift. CEO: the opportunity is 'in the multiple billions of dollars' (a TAM of '$5 billion or $10 billion or $15 billion'), early days; IBM will measure itself on signing hundreds of clients over the first many months.
quarterly_data.figure: Lightwell subscription $1 million per year; more than 7,500 package versions in first two weeks

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Arvind Krishna: 'quantum computing is no longer decades away. It is upon us, we are investing aggressively'; IBM announced plans to build Anderon, which IBM calls the world's first pure-play quantum foundry, with a $1 billion cash contribution by IBM, and disclosed plans to invest more than $10 billion in quantum over the next five years (R&D, CapEx, manufacturing scale-up, M&A, ecosystem expansion), supporting IBM's roadmap to installing in 2029 the world's first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer.
quarterly_data.figure: Anderon: $1 billion IBM cash contribution; more than $10 billion quantum investment over five years; fault-tolerant quantum computer in 2029

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Arvind Krishna: IBM is accelerating productivity actions (spend reduction, AI for software development productivity, sales and marketing effectiveness, a faster supply chain) and changes to its go-to-market model to expand coverage across thousands of additional clients beyond the Fortune 1000, including more forward-deployed engineers. CFO Jim Kavanaugh: productivity actions were ahead of plan, absorbing Confluent-related dilution; the first-half free cash flow attainment of about 30% is similar to the same point of the z16 cycle, with free cash flow margins up 300 basis points from that period.
quarterly_data.figure: free cash flow margins up 300 basis points versus the same point of the z16 cycle
